claim: There is no simple universal list of government-approved supplement brands in India, making consumer verification reliant on product-level checks rather than any central approval database.
stance_target: Government approval framework for supplements in India
quoted_support: There is not a simple universal list of all 'government-approved' supplement brands. Check the relevant regulatory information, product labelling, and manufacturer details, and verify claims through official government or brand sources.

claim: A certification logo alone on an Indian supplement does not guarantee authenticity — consumers must independently check the certification details, including underlying documentation.
stance_target: Certification logo as reliable quality signal
quoted_support: A certification logo alone does not guarantee authenticity, so check the details as well.

claim: QR codes on Indian supplement packaging cannot be relied upon as proof of authenticity because counterfeit packaging can include copied QR codes.
stance_target: QR code verification as reliable authenticity check
quoted_support: Do not rely solely on a QR code as proof of authenticity because counterfeit packaging can also contain copied codes.

claim: For Indian consumers, unusually low prices, exaggerated claims, unclear ingredient lists, poor packaging, missing batch information, and questionable seller credentials are the most common warning signs of fake or low-quality supplements.
stance_target: Consumer red flags for supplement quality in India
scope_conditions: India, online and offline supplement retail
quoted_support: Unusually low prices, exaggerated claims, unclear ingredients, poor packaging, missing batch information, and sellers with limited or questionable credentials can be warning signs.
